title: Sutra Book 2 - Dedication of Merit
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Universal Dedication, the short chant at the bottom of page one in the chant book, sung at the end of nearly every Zen ceremony and chanted tonight in Sino-Japanese. Nomon recalls learning it at the Suzuki family temple in Japan, then reads the chant line by line as three treasures: all Buddhas of ten directions and three times, Bodhisattva Mahasattvas, and Maha Prajnaparamita. Merit is described as the underlying energy of the universe, and waves on the ocean serve as the image for separateness and interconnection. Nomon compares the literal Chinese with the looser Halifax and Tanahashi translation, and ends on letting go of the merit as it is given away.

sentences.text: So last week we looked a little bit at the first thing that we chant in the evening, the robe chant, which is at the top of page one in the chant book.
Tonight I thought it would be interesting to look at the universal dedication, which is the most frequent thing that we chant.
It's at the bottom of page one.
For most people it's the first thing that you end up memorizing, and we usually don't even tell you that it's there because everyone memorizes it.
So if you didn't memorize it or didn't know where it was, you were at sea.
We usually chant it in English, and tonight was a fun exception where we chanted this little chant in Sino-Japanese.
It's done at the end of pretty much every Zen ceremony, and sometimes in the middle, too.
In English it's *all Buddhas ten directions three times.

All honored ones, Bodhisattva, Mahasattvas, Wisdom beyond Wisdom, Maha Prajnaparamita.* And then what we chanted tonight in Sino-Japanese, an early Japanese voicing of Chinese characters, which wouldn't be intelligible to a Japanese person either: *Jiho sanshi ishi fu shisonbu sa moko sa moko hoja horomi.*
We never used to chant it in Japanese ever.
What inspired me was that a group of us from the sangha went to Japan a year and a half ago, a couple years ago, and we got to stay at a temple.
It was actually the temple of the Suzuki family, where Suzuki Roshi came from in the 50s and where his son and grandson are now, and their wives.
We did a little service there with the grandson, whose name is Shungo, he's maybe about 50 years old now.
This chant came up multiple times in the service because he did a little more elaborate service, which has sections, and after each section you chant this little chant.
I was the only one that knew it, so I thought, oh, that's silly, this is an easy thing to learn, so it would be good if we all knew this.
Then you're ready when you go to Japan; at least there's one thing you'll be able to join in.
And it feels really good.
A little later we were at another big temple, and we were being hosted by some Japanese monks, and they did chant with us, the robe chant.
I remember Terrell especially, our friend Terrell, told us that shivers went up and down his spine, like, wow, it's real.
Not just made up here.
It's entirely possible we could have diverted so much over the decades here that it would be unrecognizable, but actually it sounded pretty much the same.
So this little chant at the end is an odd little chant.
What is it trying to say?
It's just kind of a list.
It says something about Buddhas, and then it says something about Bodhisattvas, and then it seems to sort of jump to a teaching, something about wisdom.
It's nouns with some enthusiastic adjectives and no verbs at all.
It doesn't say we vow, or we intend, or this is for, anything like that, so what's this about?
Well, one clue is the context of it.
It's chanted at the end of a ceremony, and it's chanted right after the chant leader, who was on tonight.
The service sounded wonderful, you three, thank you all.

Our chant leader chants something on her own, in which she makes some statements about dedicating merit, about sort of sending the energy of our chanting and bowing to teachers and beings and Bodhisattvas and stuff like that.
There it says that we dedicate the merit of this ceremony to, we're thankful for this.
It's all full sentences pretty much.
And then this is tacked on to the end.
It's at the end of not just that, but a whole pile of offerings.
First, on the community's behalf, the central priest offers incense, and already we had on the altar an offering of light, that's why there's a candle on there, and flowers, also an offering.
The incense offering is extra empowered by the priest wearing the special robe, where we learned about that last week, wearing the okesa.
In some sense the human is not that important, it's the okesa that does the offering.
The okesa needs some hands and arms, so you have to put somebody in there.
After that we all offer our whole bodies, that's what the prostration is.
It's an offering of the body, giving the body.
And then the chants.
Actually, tonight is a great example of all this, because you couldn't even understand what we were chanting for the most part.
It does all have meaning, and we usually chant most of that in English.
But the intention is not to remind ourselves of good teachings exactly.
The intention of the chanting is also an offering.
We're offering this chanting, offering these words of power, and understanding, and devotion.
So then the question comes up: who are we offering all this to?
We do have some statues that seem to create a kind of focal point, some kind of Buddha and Bodhisattva statues.
But all of it is to generate some kind of energy, which in Buddhism is called merit.
This is an interesting thing, because it's one piece of Buddhism as a religion that's been a little harder to land in our culture.

It sounds almost a little bit like a transaction, like we're generating this stuff because we have the power to generate it, and then we're kind of bequeathing it, and maybe we hope something nice will happen for us along the way.
But this is a central part of Buddhism, and always has been.

When we first received Buddhism from Asia, and of course it had already been in America for a hundred years, but when the sort of Eurocentric dominant Western culture received Buddhism from Asia, it was easy to relate to the meditation part, because it seems like we might get something from that, right?
Might get some calm or some peace.
Pretty soon we realize we also help each other by doing it together, so there's some altruism there, but we're happy to have some calm and some peace.
But all the chanting and ritual, maybe we might be a little suspicious of and a little curious about.
In fact, some people, when they first come to the Zen Center, really don't like it that much at all, and maybe you're one of them.
I'm sorry if that's the case.
Sometimes it's enough of a barrier that people say, I'll go on the other night when they don't do all that stuff, which is legit.
Tuesday and Thursday you can come, less of that.
But Buddhism really understands it as actually the most important thing.

And the other little shocker that we relearned when we went to Japan is that although we went to places where there was an emphasis on meditation for the most part, in the vast majority of Zen temples in Japan, there is not meditation actually.
There's chanting and bowing and rituals and lots of orientation also around the memorial services and funerals.
And the priest who has been trained, and the training always includes meditation.
But the message they receive is: meditation is a good thing, but your main job is this ritual.

And any priest running any temple, and often it's just one priest, maybe they have one disciple or something like that, or someone in their family who helps them, what they will do for sure every morning is bowing and chanting.
That's a lifetime commitment, and maybe some meditation before that.
So this idea of spiritual energy, of merit: the Sanskrit for it is punya.
And the Japanese is kudoku, kudoku, kudoku, which I've never really heard used.
But it's just interesting to know the word kudoku.
And the English word, as I mentioned, that was chosen to translate all this, we heard Hannah say, is merit.
So we already have some challenges whenever we translate anything, because maybe merit means something else to us than what they intended, or at least to some extent.
But merit is kind of like the underlying energy of the universe.
The idea is that it's all pervasive.
Just that you can't see it or touch it doesn't mean it's not real.
And in Western thought, we have a sort of rigid idea about what's real, right?
Maybe a little less so in other cultures.
And it's also the energy that allows the function of karma, the function of cause and effect.
And it's the energy that's really central in ethics, too.
You don't do good actions to be a good person, you do good actions because it will naturally result in good things happening in the universe.
And that happening is through this merit floating around or flowing around.
Beneficial actions generate positive merit, beneficial merit.
And I've even seen negative energy called demerit, which sounds even more funny: you got a demerit.
And of course, it's a little bit slippery, because it doesn't always look that way in the short term, this whole idea of karma, that good actions lead to good fruits.
Because who hasn't had the experience of thinking you just did something really good and something bad happened apparently as a result?
But one of the ways to look at that is that it's not just a single action and a single result, with a straight line between them.
Everything's inputs into this vast web of causality, and there's a gazillion factors that you are unaware of, including stuff inside your own mind that you're unaware of, right?
And all kinds of other things that are happening.
We only know a tiny, teeny little slice of what seems to be happening.
But the thinking is that it's all tapping into this network of energy.

And probably one of the most beneficial things we can do, maybe even more beneficial than tangible things that we would think of, ways of helping people, is to generate more positive merit, more positive energy.

And in Buddhism, which followed after the Brahminical religions of India, when the Buddha appeared, fifth century or so before the common era, religious practices are seen as like the superpower for generating merit, really effective.
Feeding children and building bridges and cleaning and all these things are also positive, but chanting a sutra is a whole other order of magnitude of goodness.
So that's why it's so important.
It's actually helping the world, very directly, be a little saner, a little happier, a little more wholesome.
It's not just a little private religious rite that will make us feel more in harmony, maybe because we're chanting together, which it does.
But it's also this intention around energy.
And maybe to us, it would sound a little bit less weird if we didn't think that we were so separate, which is another core Buddhist teaching: we're wrong about that.
We're not so separate.
We have this feeling of being a separate person.

But the more you feel into this, I think the more you realize that this temporary experience you're having, of this is me and this is what's happening with me, is actually being co-created by everybody around you.
We say, I'm influenced by others.
That's how we think about it.
But Buddhism says, yeah, no, that's not the whole story.
You're not just influenced by others, you're being created by others, created by the universe every moment.
And there's a kind of a sense of continuity, right?
And the teaching suggests, well, it seems that way, but actually it's just similar, and the next version of you just got regenerated in the next moment.
So in that universe, that way of looking at this universe, where things are much more fluid, radically impermanent and temporary, then how could there be anything but energy floating around?
There are these apparent forms, but the forms, if we really understand how insubstantial they are, how brief they are, are just little flashes of light.
A wonderful classic metaphor about all this, this distinction between separateness and interconnection or interbeing, is waves on the ocean.

The idea is that when we think we're separate, we're like the wave, a little wave moving along, looking around, saying hi to the other waves and kind of terrified of hitting the beach, because then we're gone.
But we're the ocean the whole time, the ocean the whole time.
And so this merit, this punya, is also like the water of the ocean.
And so we're improving and cleaning up and purifying the water with our rituals.
So in that frame, it seems less strange to me.
In the frame of separate mind and body, separateness, it sounds a little bit woo-woo.
But maybe everything is radically woo-woo, and it's just a description of how it is.

And that's the other thing about understanding this and understanding our ethics: you start to realize that everything we do really matters, because we're constantly interacting with this vast network of energy.
Even the way we think.
They say that the actions of body, speech and mind all generate karma, all create this energy.
Whereas in Western thought, we think that our brains are private.
So there's no privacy anymore either, sorry.
And that makes sense, right?
We know that the way we think leaks out one way or the other.
So this is just taking that up a notch: it's not just that it leaks out, it's that you're influencing the universe by what thoughts you hold.
You're co-creating the world.
So this little verse at the end seems to be a kind of coda, a punctuation mark at the end of our rituals.
It's a way for the whole sangha to add their voices to the dedication of merit, to what we're giving this merit to.
And it's actually a list of three things.
So here are the three things and the lines that point to them.
First, it says all Buddhas, ten directions.
So this is the Buddha.
There's the historical idea of the Buddha, but even early Buddhism, which had a more historical idea of the Buddha, even there, he wasn't just some guy who was really good at meditation.
That was a kind of Western cleanup job to make it less a religion, to say, oh, well, he was an ordinary person who was just really good at practice.

Even in the early Buddhist teachings, the person who became the Buddha of our age, Shakyamuni Buddha, had to practice really hard and make major sacrifices for multiple lifetimes, like hundreds of lifetimes.
So it wasn't just a "good job with your meditation" kind of thing.
But in that earlier system, there was still just one Buddha in the world at a time.
Buddhas arise and Buddhas decline.
Later Buddhism thought that's a little too narrow, a little too limited.
So in the later Mahayana Buddhism, of which we're a part, it got a lot more cosmic.
There are Buddhas everywhere: Buddhas floating around, Buddhas on flower petals, Buddhas in other worlds who can come visit this world if they get called properly.
So that's why it says all Buddhas, and ten directions means every direction: north, south, east, west, up, down, northeast, all those.
And three times means past, present and future.
The idea there is not that I'm remembering the Buddhas of the past and looking forward to the Buddhas of the future.
It's that the Buddhas of past, present and future are all right here.
And we're offering this energy, this merit, to all the Buddhas in every direction and every time.
So first we have Buddha.
And then it says Bodhisattvas Maha Sattvas.
These are Sanskrit terms.
Bodhi means awakening, sorry, and Sattva means a being.
So these are awakening beings, which has a kind of triple meaning at least.
Beings who are in the process of awakening, always.
Beings who are devoted to the awakening of others.
And those two together: awakening, awakening beings.
And Maha means great.
So Maha Sattvas is great beings.
So it's awakening beings, great beings.
And usually when they're talking about Maha Sattvas, they're talking about the sort of principle, named Bodhisattvas, of which there are somewhere between 30 and 40, depending on the system.
Bodhisattvas of compassion and Bodhisattvas of wisdom are the ones we think of the most.
Those were also mentioned in the dedication that Hannah proclaimed.
And we have a wonderful statue, pretty new to us, out in Cloud Hall, if you haven't seen it yet.
It's a Chinese version of the Bodhisattva of compassion, called in Chinese Guanyin.
So these are the Maha Sattva Bodhisattvas.
But Bodhisattva also means all of us.
It means all beings.
And in their quirky ways, and most of them wouldn't use this language, but that's okay, all beings are trying to awaken.
All beings want to be happy and don't want to suffer.
All beings want to take care of each other and help their children.
And we can think of plenty of examples of beings that seem to do that in a ridiculously distorted way, but nonetheless, that's our understanding.
These beings are trying to awaken in their own way.
There are also some deep teachings about greed, hate and delusion, but we'll save that for another day.
I think that might come in in a couple weeks.
Yeah, yeah.
So this is the Sangha, the Sangha writ large.
We had Buddha, and we had Sangha, the community, the Bodhisattvas.
And then it jumps to wisdom beyond wisdom, Maha Prajnaparamita.
Suddenly now we're talking about what seems to be a teaching.

What's meant here is really respecting and paying homage to not just a particular teaching, but a way of understanding the universe in the light of this radical, interpenetrated impermanence beyond anything that we can quite understand with our big brains.
So wisdom beyond wisdom is just an English translation of Prajnaparamita.
And there's Maha again: great.
So great Prajnaparamita.

Wisdom not like a bunch of information, but wisdom like a deep understanding and a radical openness and allowing of everything to actually be its interpenetrated, flowing, impermanently, constantly reappearing state.
And that's the universe in which all this makes sense.
So it makes a lot of sense that we would then go to the Dharma in that way.
Our little verse does have the three treasures.
They're not in the usual order, Buddha, Sangha and then Dharma.
And all of this is to remind us of a couple of things.
The teachings of not-self, which I've been alluding to: that there's something much bigger going on here than any idea I could have of me or you or us or anything.
And this is also reminding us of how important our choices are.
What are we adding to these fields of energy?
Are we adding our good hearts, chanting and bowing?
Are we adding kindness?
Are we adding narrow-mindedness?
Are we adding reactivity?
And all of that's always present in the room, because we're humans.
But we can think about that when you feel a little judgmental of your neighbors chanting or something, like, ah, shoot, spiking the offering.
Well, wow, because it really matters even just to think that.
Yeah, my collective offering gets a little bit.
So if you look very literally at the Chinese, it's even briefer.
I'm struggling a little bit because I forgot my readers.
Oh, you have some?
Oh, that's handy.
Somewhere I have this.
That's just kind of letting my notes remind me what I want to say.
Thank you so much.
So all this stuff comes to us from all the canonical texts written down in Chinese, pronounced in an unusual way, as I mentioned, by the Japanese monks, and I found it here.
The literal translation of the underlying Chinese goes like this.
Okay, here we go, I found it.
*Ten directions, three times, all Buddhas, venerable Bodhisattva, Mahasattvas, Maha Prajnaparamita.*
So that's pretty close to what we say.
We have a little bit of mirroring between the English and the Sanskrit: instead of just Maha Prajnaparamita, we have wisdom beyond wisdom, Maha Prajnaparamita.
But it does have this problem, right?
It doesn't really explain itself.
When you're translating and bringing something into a new culture, you have to figure out how much we should improve it so it makes sense to us.
And this one, the way we do it, is pretty literal.
One of my sources for this talk is a little book, which I meant to bring and forgot, by Kazuaki Tanahashi, known as KAAS.

He shares that in the translation he did with Roshi Joan Halifax for the Upaya Zen Center in New Mexico, which some of us have been to, an important Zen center in the American scene, they went with "let's have this make sense to us."
So they translated it as,
*All awaken one throughout space and time, honored ones, great beings who help all to awaken together.
We realize wisdom beyond wisdom.*
Isn't that interesting?
Quite different, but the same ideas.
That's a much looser translation.
The Chinese characters for "realize" and "together help" aren't there.
Those are all additions so that it makes sense.
So it's always a question: how much do we tweak it, and how much do we just have something a little mysterious?
And then once a decade or so we'll give a Dharma talk and explain it again.
If you miss that talk, you'll never know.
I feel pretty good about the choices we've inherited: pretty true to the original, but a little more English, so it makes a little sense, and it makes sense once you learn about it.
So that's what we're doing when we add that little chant at the end.
We're reminding ourselves and each other of the fluidity and spaciousness and freedom of our true nature, and that we're all part of this ocean of energy.
At this moment, as we chant, we're waves dancing, but we're going to drop right back into the ocean any second.
Since we get to be waves, we get to manifest something.
We get to choose what comes out of our mouths.
And so we choose joyfully this offering, the strengthening of generosity and giving and wisdom.
We might think of this closing part, the very end of our merit making, as: I let go of myself as I give away this merit.
And the wisdom [unclear: "we on"] wisdom part reminds us that there's no one here to make merit, no one to hold on to merit, and no merit to give away.
That's why we can give away the merit.
It's that sense of freedom.
So it's not just "Hey guys, here you go."
It's wisdom beyond wisdom.
So that's what I wanted to say tonight.
Interesting, all these little gems embedded in the thing.
Huh?
Do you have any questions or thoughts or additions?
Can you guys hear online through the room, Mike?
Or do we need to?
Okay, cool.
**Participant:** Yeah.
So I kind of carry that idea of merit as something that you have attained, and cautioned about attainment.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** So you brought a different meaning to the word.
Yeah, it's not something we can attain.
It's more something that's emergent, more process than thing.
**Participant:** Yeah.
Our hearts.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
Thanks.
Oh, yeah, that's exactly right.
That's what it is.
That's one of the ways that merit is problematic for us: giving a merit badge.
And sure, there's some boy scouts in the room.
Nothing wrong with that.
But [unclear: "curl scouts"], that's a virtuous activity.
Yeah.
Thanks.
I mean, the merit thing, it's all over the place.
We talk about good vibes and energy, the Indians talk about Prana, and the East Asian traditions talk about Chi.
So there's lots of energy stuff going on.
If you've ever participated in any of the healing modalities that use energy, which science cannot understand or describe, and you feel something, it's like, well, there's something here.
You're gonna say something, Chris.
**Participant:** So beyond.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Tim, we can't hear what's happening in the room.
Chris, I'm gonna repeat it.
Hold on a sec.
Yeah, no worries.
So Chris Burkhart is saying it just points to the vastness of what we're doing when we do this chanting ritual stuff.
It's like reminding ourselves that this is beyond anything.
It's beyond our thought, it's past, present, it's beyond time, it's beyond space.
Is that a pretty good summary?
It's a pointing to the beyondness of the whole thing.
So yeah, we have to be disciplined about passing microphones around, or I'll just repeat.
It's fine either way.
Are you feeling uplifted and beyond?
I hope so.
A little more so.
Okay.
So anyway, the other thing that's interesting is that you don't have to believe anything, right?
Because belief would be a rigid thing in your brain anyway.
So it's better if you don't believe any of this.
Just do it.
And a more traditional thing in this [unclear: "end world"] is you never explain any of this anyway, right?
You just follow along, you'll figure it out.
Okay.
That's good for now.
Huh?
Thank you so much for listening.
I'm on a roll, and I've got some Confederates lined up here too, if I'm out of town.
But I think we'll keep going, a deep dive through the sutra book.
